```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(csquares)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
```

When working with grid encoding systems like CSquares, you should be aware of
boundary cases. This is demonstrated with a set op evenly distributed points:

```{r define-points}
pts <-
  expand.grid(
    x = seq(-0.11, 0.11, by = 0.01),
    y = seq(-0.11, 0.11, by = 0.01)
  ) |>
  sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 4326)
```

Note that some of these points are exactly on CSquare cell boundaries, depending
on the selected resolution. So, what happens with these points when assigning
them to specific CSquare cells? Let's see:

```{r to-csquares}
csq <- as_csquares(pts, resolution = 0.05)
plot(csq, axes = TRUE)
```

If we count the number of points in each Csquare cell you will notice something
interesting.

```{r summarise}
csq_agg <- summarise(csq |> group_by(csquares), count = n())
plot(csq_agg["count"], axes = TRUE)
```

You will see an artifact near the Equator and at the Prime Meridian. Even though
the points are distributed homogeneously over space, lower number of points
are counted near these lines. Why is this?

This is because of how Rees (2015) defined boundary cases for assigning CSquares
codes to geo-referenced points: it follows a strict "lower-limit inclusive" convention.

Any grid encoding system would suffer from some form of boundary assumptions and
artifacts. This often occurs at the edges of the area covered by the system.
But in case of the CSquares, this occurs near the Prime Meridian and Equator.

## When worry about boundary effect?

When locations are measured with precision that causes data to snap to CSquare cell
bounds. This could cause an issue. The same is true if there are physical bounds
or other reasons for the data to snap to cell bounds. This is true for any
grid encoding system. So, you should never encode data to a resolution that
surpasses your data precision

If your measured locations are affected by random processes and is sufficiently
precise, points will fall on either side of a cell boundary. Cases where they
are exactly on the boundary should be extremely rare.

So this becomes especially a challenge when the number of locations is limited
and / or when the required resolution is fine compared to location precision.

## Handling boundary effects

If your data for some reason snaps exactly to cell boundaries, you could add
some jitter to the location (only a fraction of the resolution of your grid),
causing the point to randomly fall on either side of the boundary. To understand
if and how this affects your analysis, you could perform a Monte Carlo simulation
with the jittering.

If you don't want these artifacts to occur near the Prime Meridian or Equator,
you could also chose to convert your CSquares grid to a
[stars](https://r-spatial.github.io/stars/) object, and drop the CSquares encoding.
You can then use `sf::st_within` or `sf::st_intersects` to assign points
to the cells. Whichever method you chose, always document what you have done and
why.

Furthermore, the selection of a appropriate scale for your grid encoding is key.
You should always be aware effects cell size can have on your data processing.

## References

 * Rees, T. (2015); ""C-Squares," A New Spatial Indexing
   System and its Applicability to the Description of
   Oceanographic Datasets" Oceanography 16(1), 11-19
   <https://doi.org/10.5670/oceanog.2003.52>
